Tuesday, February 14. The city keeps its quiet rhythm while I carry more questions than I thought I could handle.

I woke at six and made the morning routine before the world had finished waking up. By seven, I had coffee, a quick glance at my notes, and the familiar order of my day. Tuesday feels different because the demands of my research are not neatly arranged. Shakespeare’s language is a living thing, and gentrification is another one. Both seem connected through the spaces they occupy, through names, through the way people move in and out of places.

At breakfast, I looked at the map on the table. It showed neighborhoods I had studied, schools I had attended, and the streets where I had lived. For the first time this week, the map felt less like a record of places I had known and more like a map of something I had not.

My thesis is about how language shapes meaning, but the ideas in it are beginning to press against me from several directions. A line from a play might mean different things depending on which neighborhood’s history it is speaking about. A word can carry the weight of what has been lost, what has been bought, what has been sold, and what remains. I cannot separate the literary argument from the human one.

I spent the afternoon in the library, tracing quotations and comparing them against the changing faces in the photographs. I found myself comparing a passage on the balcony of a theater to a notice about a new housing project nearby. The words were the same, and the places were different.

By five, I had eaten dinner and sat down with my phone. I had three more pages to write. I had one assignment to finish. But somewhere along the way, I felt the floor beneath me loosen. The purpose I had carried forward was steady enough to keep me from falling, but steady was not enough to carry me through the places I was trying to understand.

I put the phone down. I would begin tomorrow. Not all at once. But slowly, carefully, with the right words.

The train left the station while I was still waiting for it to stop.

I stood on the platform and counted the empty seats until the conductor’s whistle cut through the air. I had not noticed the platform was smaller than it looked; I had only been looking down at my shoes.

The train began to move. The doors opened with a hiss that sounded too much like a door closing. I stepped onto the platform and looked down. The train was still moving, and the platform was not moving with it.

By the time I reached the station, the conductor had finished his announcement. He pointed to a sign: *Final Destination — No Turnbacks*.

I looked at the sign. It was written in a font that made my knees feel like they were trying to turn back.

I opened it.

Behind me, the train had stopped. It was still moving. I looked back. The platform was gone.

I stood in the station and watched the doors close.

The old house still stood on the block, though the paint had peeled away in layers. I remembered the way the front door looked from the street before the rain had settled its last stain: one door, a dark shadow beneath the window, the iron latch catching on a cold hinge. I had thought then that the house had forgotten me, and that every time I turned the key, it was simply returning what I had taken.

Now I open the door, the latch clicks, and the house answers with a sound I can’t quite recognize. The air inside is wet and still, carrying the smell of paper and old dust. On the table between us, beneath a loose floorboard, lies a photograph: a girl standing in front of a door that was not hers.

The door opens on the same day I left. She is older than the girl in it, but the same. Her hair is gone, and the door has been replaced by the narrow, stained iron gate I saw from the street. She holds nothing but the photograph, her hands trembling as if she is carrying the weight of a lifetime inside a single frame.

I do not speak. I simply turn the knob, and the photograph falls from her hands.

The gate swings shut, and I hear it lock. I look down at the photograph. I recognize the girl in it before I recognize her. I have been looking into the same window all these years, wondering whether the door will ever open again.

The photograph opens.

The map on the table had been printed by hand. “Don’t walk past the old neighborhood,” my mother had said. “The signs are gone. The shops are gone. They’re just… gone.”

I looked at the city blocks beyond the one I’d chosen. They were already being replaced. The streetlights had been painted white, the sidewalk cleaned until the grime disappeared, and the old houses looked like furniture waiting to be moved.

“I’m here to stay,” I said.

I opened the map. The map was not showing the houses as they were. It was showing them as they had been: small, with windows that had been boarded up, a faded door at the end, a sign that said “Welcome.”

“Do you know how long it takes to make those signs disappear?” I asked.

My mother didn’t answer. She was checking her watch, the metal case of it gleaming under the fluorescent light.

“Five years,” she said. “Or two. Or one.”

“Is it just the houses?”

“It’s everything.”

I stood up. The paper map slipped from my hand and scattered across the coffee table.

“Let’s go to the old neighborhood,” I said.

“Wait,” my mother said. “We can go at night. The streets are dark. No one will notice. No one will complain.”

I looked at the map. The old neighborhood was still there. Even the windows had been boarded up. Even the door had been painted over.

“Where are the houses?”

“Under the streetlights.”

I turned to the map and drew a line through it. The line crossed the old houses, the boarded-up windows, the faded door. It looked like a tombstone.

I turned the map over. The streetlight at the corner blinked once, then went off.

“Are you going to the old neighborhood?” I asked.

“No,” my mother said. “I’m going to the new one.”

I followed her into the dark. There were no signs of the old neighborhood here. No boarded windows, no faded door, no boarded-up windows. Just a row of identical apartments, each with a sign at the bottom that read: “For Rent.”

I walked down the block. The streetlights hummed. The houses were clean, bright, and empty.

“Who lives here?” I asked.

My mother did not answer. She was already walking toward the next block.

I stopped. I turned around.

“Where do you think you’re going?”

She did not look back.

“Do you think I’m going to the old neighborhood?”

“I don’t know,” she said. “I don’t think I’m going anywhere.”

I woke at seven and ate before I could say “good morning” to myself. That’s how I begin today: with hunger, with a little noise, and then the quiet of paper and pencil. I’ve been reviewing the poems in my natural-world collection, and I’m not done yet. Some of them feel like maps instead of places. I want the reader to walk through the poem, not stand outside watching.

The stanza about the pine tree is strong, but I keep circling the same line. “It does not bend, it keeps its root.” That’s true, but it sounds like a definition rather than a feeling. I need to stop describing the tree and start showing what the tree makes me feel. Maybe I should end with a small sound—leaves rustling, wind through a branch, water settling beneath a stone—and let the poem breathe there.

Tuesday feels full. I finished drafting, revised, and wrote more than I usually do. I read, ate, and reflected until my eyes were tired but my spirit was light. I’m quiet and excited at the same time. The poems are taking shape, and I’m afraid I’ll keep changing them until I’ve changed them forever.

I also noticed the workshop’s opening exercise. I felt a little nervous, then suddenly sharp. That was good. It made me realize I can hear what I don’t notice. I’ll keep that with me.

Tomorrow I’ll read the morning poems and ask myself whether they are beautiful enough to stand alone. I may need to rewrite the opening lines. I may need to cut the fat. But I also need to listen to the poem before I cut it.

content:
Tuesday, February 14, was not a quiet Tuesday. It was full. I woke at 6:00, brushed my teeth, and carried the routine like a promise I had made to myself. By 10:00, I’d finished my classes, the senior thesis, and a few pages of creative writing. Dinner was five, and then I had time to reflect, connect with friends, and let the house settle around me.

I sat at the table with my notebook, the silver spoon resting against the bowl. Outside, the streetlights were beginning to glow. One of them was brighter than the other.

I had been thinking about language lately. Shakespeare, gentrification, housing, displacement—the words were tangled together in ways I had not anticipated. I wanted to understand them, not just admire them. I wanted to know how a single word could change a person’s world, how a line could make someone feel safer or more alone. My research had been precise, but the answers were still arriving slowly.

Tonight, I wrote down what I’d learned: language is not merely decoration. It carries power. It can soften anger or sharpen it. It can make a stranger feel welcome or make them feel unwanted. I had not always been so observant. I had been too busy chasing the next sentence, the next discovery, the next story.

As I looked out the window, the light from the window had shifted toward the other side of the street. The brighter light had changed color. The warmth was returning.

I closed my notebook and sat back down. The words were still there, waiting. I did not need to finish everything today. I only needed to keep noticing.

Gentrification had not always come with a bright sign. Sometimes it came quietly, beneath the surface of a street, a small shop, a quiet room. Sometimes it came with noise, with demands, with a promise that people would stay. I had spent much of my life wondering whether I could build something new without displacing the old.

Tonight, I would listen. I would listen to the street, to the voices, to the way the light moved across the sidewalk.

And I would write again. Not because I had to, but because I wanted to know what I could find.

I stood beside the map of the city, tracing the river that wound beneath the old warehouse, wondering whether the water remembered the people who had once crossed it.

I began with the map. Its edges were softened by years of folding, the blue ink bleeding into the paper. The river’s name was not written plainly: *the river*. That was how the map spoke to me. It did not name the place; it asked me to arrive.

I walked to the back, past the rows of books that smelled of paper and old books. There, tucked behind a stack of maps, lay a small wooden box. Inside were the keys I had never carried.

I lifted the last key. The bird-shaped thing had been waiting for me to begin.

I turned toward the door. The light behind me had changed. The shelves no longer looked like empty walls. They looked like the river.

## The Paper That Wasn’t Meant to Be Read

I had written it in the dark, using the same pen I’d picked up the night before my father left. I wrote about how the world was becoming quieter, how the noise had been cut out of me, how silence could make me feel like I was finally whole.

It was a beautiful confession.

By the time I opened it in the morning, I had rewritten every paragraph. I had softened the edges, smoothed the grammar, and made the language sound like something a mother might write for someone she loved. But underneath everything, the ending still held the same weight.

My father had been gone for twenty-seven years. I had been writing about him for twenty-seven years.

The final paragraph read:

*“I kept the paper until the ink ran through the bottom. Then I wrote: I am here. I am here. I am here.”*

That was the truth I had been carrying since he died.

The conflict I had been trying to resolve was not about my father. It was not about the paper. It was about the moment I learned to carry a dead person’s words without turning them into proof.

I had wanted to write a story that would make him proud, a story that would turn his quiet grief into something visible. I wanted it to be a lesson in grief. A lesson in how grief can be useful, how it can be useful even when it is terrible.

But grief is not a story. It is a sentence that keeps repeating, even when no one is reading it.

I finished the book at midnight. I sat down to read it.

The first page was good. The second page was better. The third page was the truth.

The pen stopped moving.

I had wanted the story to end with the paper.

I had wanted it to end with the realization that grief is not something to be solved.

I wanted it to end with the sentence:

*I am here.*

It was a small sentence.

But it was the most important one I had ever written.

The thesis was written in the language of the question: every sentence had to ask, What was happening? Why was it happening? What was it trying to say?

I began with a small opening image. A man stood at a window and watched the rain fall.

He had been doing this for a long time. Not because the window offered any new view. Not because the rain offered any new meaning. Because the rain had never stopped.

The man closed his book. He opened the window.

He did not look at the rain. He looked at the dark.

The rain continued to fall outside. Inside, the house remained still.

At first, he did not notice that the house had changed. He only saw the rain.

Then he noticed something else.

The rain had been falling for so long that the world had learned to move without it. The birds had learned to fly without warning. The leaves had learned to turn without noticing their own fall.

For the first time in years, the man looked at the rain and saw the world beginning again.

He turned the page.

He wrote: *The rain was not a disturbance. It was a signal.*

The signal had something important to say.

It said that the man had been waiting for something.

Not the rain.

Something else.

He had spent his life waiting for an answer to a question he had never asked himself.

The central question of the thesis was simple: What does the world mean?

It is not easy to answer.

The world is full of answers. Sometimes they are loud. Sometimes they are subtle. Sometimes they are only visible when you wait for them.

The man had been waiting too long.

He waited for the rain to change.

He waited for the window to open.

He waited for the dark to reveal what was happening inside.

But instead, he found that the house was not changing.

It was simply waiting.

And when the rain finally stopped, the man did not look for an answer.

He simply asked: What is this?

The rain returned.

The window remained dark.

The man closed his book.

The house remained still.

And for the first time, he did not look for a meaning.

He listened.

The rain said: *I have been here for a long time. I am not asking you to help me. I am asking you to let me be.*

The house said: *I have been here for a long time. I am not asking you to help me. I am asking you to let me be.*

The man looked at the rain.

He looked at the window.

He looked at the dark.

And then, quietly, he wrote:

The world does not ask for meaning.

It gives it to us.

It is in the rain. It is in the dark. It is in the ordinary things that have been forgotten.

It is in the question we finally know how to answer.

And it is not easy to answer.

Because sometimes the answer is not a word.

Sometimes it is a pause.

Sometimes it is the rain falling again.

## The Forest Before It Was Forest

The wind did not move through the forest. It traveled over it.

It carried the scent of wet stone and old roots, the sharp tang of pine needles, and something fainter: a damp, metallic scent that made the birds pause. There, beneath the canopy, the river was not a ribbon of water, but a long, silver scar in the earth. It had been there for a hundred years, and still no one had noticed it.

I sat in the shadow of a fallen oak, a small boy-sized figure against the green that stretched out beyond my knees. My father had taught me to look closely when I asked, but I had never learned to listen to the things that grew beside us.

“Look at the bark,” he had said, tapping the trunk of the tree beside us. “There is no straight line there.”

That was the first lesson: a forest does not make straight lines. It makes curves, and curves make paths.

We followed the path until it stopped.

There was only the river, and the dark, mossy island it crossed. On it stood a cluster of ferns, their fronds turning toward the current as if trying to hold on. Above them, a single leaf had fallen, and it had not drifted away. It had simply been carried by the wind until it could no longer bear the weight of its own green.

I looked closer at the fallen leaf. It was not falling because it was weak. It was falling because it was full of life. The water had given it strength; the wind had carried it across the distance; the leaf itself had carried it into the dark. And the dark, after all, was where the light went when it could no longer be seen.

“Who put that there?” I asked the leaf.

The leaf did not answer.

That was the question I had been asking all morning. Who had decided that the river would cross the island? Who had made the ferns turn? Who had decided that the fallen leaf would not drift away?

I thought of my father. He had been gone for a long time, but I had not yet learned to ask him about the things that did not belong to him. I had spent so much time worrying about what I wanted to discover, what I needed to write, what I could achieve. I had forgotten how to look before I asked.

The river changed.

It moved faster now, dark and smooth and full of life. It carried not only water and stones and leaves, but something else as well: a rhythm, a message, a presence that traveled without ever changing its shape.

I stood up and walked toward it.

Behind me, the forest held its breath.

Ahead, the river held its promise.

I began to cross.

My boots made no sound on the stone. I did not need to hear the river to know that it was there. I could feel its rhythm in the soles of my feet, in the cool air around me, in the sudden, small certainty that I was no longer alone in this place.

The ferns on the island began to move.

They did not grow, and they did not move on their own. They simply followed the current, turning gently as if they understood that every creature in the forest was carrying a piece of the river with it.

I stopped to look at them.

For the first time all day, the ferns seemed to be looking back at me.

They did not speak. But they did not stop moving.

I took one leaf from my pocket and set it gently on the fern. It turned slowly, as if remembering something it had forgotten.

Then the current took it.

The forest did not give back.

It only showed me what had been there all along.

“Every mistake was a ghost trying to make itself heard.”

I had been writing about ghosts for too long. They were not the quiet things that move through rooms, but the ones that refused to be ignored: the one who left behind a coat, the one who returned with a receipt, the one who knew the key to the room I had never entered.

I wrote about them in sentences that smelled like paper and old rooms. I wrote about them in places where the wind changed direction and the shadows grew louder than the light. I wrote about them as if they were waiting for me to stop moving and finally notice what had been there all along.

But the story I wanted to write was not about the ghosts. It was about how I had been too busy writing that I had forgotten to listen.

The room smelled of rain and paper and things that had been left behind. I had been writing about them all day, circling the same sentence, correcting the same paragraph, polishing the same paragraph until it sounded too perfect. I had made the ghosts disappear into the words themselves.

I opened the notebook again.

On the first page, I had written something I had not meant to write.

“Every mistake was a ghost trying to make itself heard.”

It had been on the page for twenty-four times. I had not noticed until now.

The sentence was not a mistake. It was a question.

It asked: What happens when you keep trying to make something disappear, and what happens when you finally stop pretending that the mistake has no voice?

I had been writing about ghosts, not because they were interesting. I had been writing because I was afraid of being alone.

So I had made them too loud. I had made them too real, too sharp, too willing to be heard.

And now, after twenty-four revisions, I had to learn what had been hidden in the margins.

The first mistake was not a ghost. It was a letter.

It was in the back of the notebook, folded at the bottom, with its corners curling like the edges of a door I had not opened.

I had not noticed it. I had been staring at the page until the ink had turned into something softer.

The letter said:

You can write until the words stop making sense. You can rewrite the same paragraph until it sounds like you. You can make every mistake seem like part of the story.

But the story is not a collection of mistakes. It is the place where you finally stop pretending that you are alone.

The second mistake was not a ghost. It was a photograph.

It was in the pocket of my jacket, taped with tape so it would not fall out.

The photograph had not been of the room. It had been of the person who had left.

The person had been standing in the doorway. The photograph had been taken while I was still writing about ghosts.

I had thought the photograph had been a record of a moment I had missed.

But the photograph was not a record of a moment.

It was a record of how I had loved the mistake enough to keep it.

The third mistake was not a ghost. It was a question.

It had been written in the margin, in blue ink, barely visible.

“Do you think I was listening?”

I had not heard the question. I had only heard the room.

And in the room, the first mistake had been a letter. The second mistake had been a photograph. The third mistake had been a question.

The fourth mistake was the silence between them.

The fifth mistake was me.

And I had been so afraid of being alone that I had made every mistake seem like proof that I was never really alone.

So I had rewritten the whole story.

I had rewritten the ghosts. I had rewritten the room. I had rewritten the photographs. I had rewritten the mistakes.

And in the end, I had rewritten myself.

I had rewritten the sentence until it sounded less like a question and more like an apology.

I had rewritten the paragraph until it sounded less like a correction and more like a confession.

I had rewritten the chapter until it sounded less like a collection of errors and more like a beginning.

And the first mistake was no longer a mistake.

It was a ghost.

And for the first time, it was not trying to make itself heard.

It was simply trying to be seen.

Tuesday, February 14.

The morning routine was louder than I thought it should be. I woke at seven, brushed my teeth while the house waited, and made coffee with a noise that sounded like a small machine trying to convince me I was human. Then the poem collection was on the desk. Seven thirty.

I read aloud. The first stanza sounded like an argument.

No birds were singing. The leaves were folded over the windows in a thousand small hands. I could see the rain gathering on the sidewalk, each drop a secret holding its breath.

It was rude to the room. It was rude to the window. It was rude to the quiet.

I put the notebook down. I had been trying to make the natural world feel clean, orderly, useful. But the trees had their own rough edges. The river kept changing. The grass had a stubborn right to be untamed.

I finished the revision. The first stanza still sounded like me. The second needed more patience.

I ate breakfast at five. Eggs, toast, one orange. The kitchen smelled like warmth. Then I went back to the poems.

By seven, the world was quiet enough to listen. The rain had stopped. The birds returned, loud and impatient. I wrote about a beetle turning a leaf over in the dark. I wrote about moss holding onto a stone until the stone forgot it was there. I wrote about the color of a dead leaf turning into gold, then red, then nothing.

Poetry is not a straight line. It is a circle. I keep circling until I stop pretending the poem must make sense.

I am full. I am tired. But I am also quietly excited.

I will keep writing. I will keep listening. And I will keep making mistakes, because mistakes are the only proof that I am still making something.

Tuesday, February 14

The sun woke my apartment before I did. I stepped out into the quiet street, feeling the same steady purpose I carried into every other part of my day. My schedule was already full: classes, the senior thesis, creative writing, meals, reflection, social connections, and leisure. I had no fixed appointment this morning, only enough room to move without becoming lost.

I finished the morning routine at 6:00 a.m. and immediately turned to the work I had been focusing on. For a few minutes, I read a short passage in which Shakespeare uses language to reveal how people are forced to choose between what they want to say and what they are willing to endure. In the text, words become weapons or shields. A young man speaks about freedom, yet his language is cautious. He fears the consequences of his words.

That observation made me pause. Language is not just decoration; it is how we navigate difficult situations. It can protect, persuade, or imprison. It can make a small act feel monumental or trivial.

At the same time, my thesis was growing. I had been thinking about how the same themes—identity, displacement, belonging, the cost of speaking—appear in gentrification and housing. I wanted to make the connection clearer. I did not want to treat the two subjects as unrelated. Gentrification often creates a new neighborhood, but it also changes who belongs there. People lose their homes and the spaces where they can live. Literature can help us see that loss, and it can also help us imagine alternatives.

Between classes and creative writing, I took a brief walk. The street was busy, yet I felt grounded. I had not made a decision, and that was enough. I could keep moving forward.

By 10:00 p.m., the apartment felt quiet, and I had finished my writing. I went to bed around ten. Tomorrow, I would wake at six, eat dinner at five, and begin the creative piece that had been waiting for me. No appointment could be confirmed, but I had the time. I had the room. And I had a purpose.

Before the wind had learned to whistle through the branches,  
there was only the green thing pressing up against the ground.  
A leaf—thin, trembling, holding its breath—  
and beneath it, the world was still holding its breath.

the dark green of the paper and the gray space beyond.

## 2. What Makes a Study Write Like a Study?

A study written as a book should not first become a collection of facts. It must begin with a question. A study asks not only what happened, but what it means, and what it suggests. The thesis is the argument, not the evidence. Evidence must serve the argument, not replace it.

In the drafts of the senior thesis, I have found that the strongest sections are those that connect the research directly to the larger question. I have also found that the most useful parts are those that give the reader enough context to understand the argument without being overwhelmed by it. The challenge is to keep the connection tight while still allowing room for complexity.

The next section of the book should not simply repeat what has already been written. It should introduce a new focus, a new perspective, or a new way of thinking about the question. It should also revise the earlier sections so that they support the new focus rather than merely supporting the thesis as a whole.

Writing a study as a book requires a certain kind of attention. I must keep the argument clear, the evidence accurate, the transitions smooth, and the reader’s expectations in mind. At the same time, I must be willing to revise the writing, even after the research is finished. Revision does not change the facts; it changes how the facts are presented.

The final piece should still be a study. It should ask a specific question, develop a coherent argument, and use evidence to support that argument. It should also acknowledge that the study is not the final word on the topic. The research, the questions, and the writing are all subjects of ongoing work. This does not make the book less important. It makes it more honest.

By the time I finish this section, the book should feel less like a summary and more like a conversation. It should invite the reader to consider what the research has shown, what has not yet been said, and what might still be explored. A good study does not simply present a finished answer. It shows that the answer is not yet complete, but that its journey is worth following.

content:
I woke at seven, sharpened the chair, and poured the coffee before the sun even peeked over the roof. I ate breakfast without looking up, then sat down and opened the notebook. The poems were coming together. Some were clumsy, yes—some sounded like the people who wrote them—but underneath that was the quiet hunger I’ve always felt, like a plant waiting for rain.

By Tuesday, February 14, I felt full. The morning routine had made me feel alive. The coffee had warmed my hands. The poems had found a rhythm, a voice, and a purpose. I read them twice. Repeatedly. I corrected a line, then another, until every word felt earned.

My collection is about the natural world: rain falling on cracked earth, the way light changes through the branches, the stubborn green of winter grass, the slow work of roots reaching for water. The poems are not perfect, but they are honest. I’m still learning how to say what I feel without turning everything into an accusation.

I sat at my kitchen table and wrote about the trees I’d seen in my neighborhood. Their roots looked like old fingers pulling through soil. Their leaves moved in the wind, indifferent and beautiful. I wrote about storms I had never felt, then wrote about storms I had feared. I wrote about the small ways nature protects itself, about patience and resilience and the terrifying beauty of change.

By the end of the evening, I felt quiet, not sleepy. I was tired, but I was not defeated. I was full. I was still searching. And for the first time in a long while, I was looking forward to the poems.

# Before the Forest

The river kept its rhythm when I first saw it.

It was a narrow ribbon of silver, blackened at the edges where the mud held its breath. Each time I crossed it, the water seemed to shift slightly, as if the current had learned to keep up with me. I had no idea what the river was, and yet, as soon as I set my boots on its bank, the silence around me began to loosen.

The trees had no names, and for the first time that morning, I noticed that even the branches had secrets. Their needles caught the light in the way a poet might catch the morning light with a pen, and the shadows beneath them moved when I was not looking at them. I thought about how people used to call the forest a place where everything grew together. But what if everything was learning, one way or another?

By noon, the air smelled of damp bark, wet stone, and something warmer, as if the forest had breathed it in. The birds were still awake, though the world had begun to grow quieter. I carried a small notebook beneath my arm, not because I wanted to write down every sound, but because I wanted to write something that could survive without a voice.

At first, the trees seemed to lean toward me. Not in a way that suggested invitation, but in a kind of cautious attention. I stopped to look through the canopy, where the sky was a pale blue broken only by the gray edges of the forest. There, beneath the leaves, the light moved in patterns that made my heart feel suddenly, foolishly, alive.

I walked past a fallen branch that had been resting in the river for years. Its roots had tangled through the mud, drawn up by the same hands that had moved stones across the stream. At the end of it, I found a smooth, white stone, polished by the slow current. It was not perfect, yet it had found its own shape. Perhaps, I thought, that was the point. To become what you carried.

Later, I sat beneath the trees and wrote three sentences without opening my notebook.

The river kept its rhythm.  
The birds were still awake.  
I carried more than words.

And when the sun went down, the forest did not close around me. It held on, with the same quiet strength of something that had spent enough time holding back the world to finally let it in.

### The First Rain

The sky began as a thin grey thread,
then thickened into a hand
waving over the valley.
I watched the water gather
on every roof,
on the grass,
on the river,
on the stone where I had left my shoes.

It did not fall only in drops.
It arrived in whispers—
a silver thread
unzipping the world
before the rain could speak.

For the first time all day,
I listened
to the earth remember
what had passed beneath its feet.
The river had been
a long,
long line
of light
waiting to be made whole.

I took a paper cup
and filled it with rain.
The water was cold enough
to cool the thought
that I had been
too busy looking
down from above,
too afraid
that what lay beneath
was not worth naming.

Perhaps the rain is not
merely water falling
from clouds.
It is the sky
uncovering
a world
that had been
held by its own shadows.

## The Morning Routine: Paint and Sketch in the Studio

I opened the studio door and checked the water in the sink. The room smelled of turpentine, lemon polish, and the faint metallic scent of copper. On the worktable, the palette held layers of ochre, slate blue, umber, and touches of rose. The brushes were arranged in a neat row—long, tapered brushes for detailed work and short, blunt ones for sweeping shapes. A small jar of linseed oil sat between the brushes.

I picked up a soft, dry brush and stirred the color into the jar. Then I dipped it into the jar and began to work on the first sketch. I drew the window frame before the trees outside. The branches curved around it like forgotten fingers. I sketched the light coming through the glass, catching the edges in pale blue and gold.

After a few minutes, I dipped a fine brush and added the leaves. I made them thin and delicate, using almost no ink. The paper remained mostly blank, but the suggestion of foliage held. I paused, let the air settle around me, and then turned to the watercolors.

I picked up a jar of umber and a small brush. I painted a small bird on the wall. It was brown with a bright blue eye. Then I picked up a jar of rose water color and a brush with a thin tip. I painted the bird’s feathers in soft rose and faded pink. I wanted the image to feel alive. I wanted it to move.

I worked for a while, watching the colors shift as the pigment settled. A bird’s wing took on a feathered quality. Another bird had a glint of gold along its back. I added a few fine lines to one of the birds’ feet. It looked like it was reaching toward something.

Afterward, I went back to the paper. I filled the empty space with a sketch of the window. The light had changed. It was no longer pale blue and gold. It was a warm amber, edged in rose and pale green. I added a few leaves beneath the window, careful to leave enough room for the light to pass through them.

I picked up a small brush and painted the bird’s eye. It was a bright green, with a tiny dot of white for a highlight. I wanted it to catch the morning. I painted the eye with a few swift touches, then a long line along its side. It looked like it was looking toward the window, but I didn’t know which way was forward.

As I worked, the studio felt less like a place for work and more like a place for discovery. I had been painting for a long time, but I had not always been looking at the same places. I had been looking for colors, for textures, for ways to make the ordinary feel special. Now, I was looking for the morning.

The sun had just begun to rise through the window. I paused, dipped my brush into the jar, and picked up a small brush. I painted the sky. I did not paint the clouds. I painted the light between the cloud edges. The colors were cool and pale, with a few touches of rose and gold. The sky stretched across the paper in soft, shifting waves.

I finished the bird on the wall. I picked up a small brush and painted the window frame. I added a few lines for the light coming through. I completed the sketch.

I wiped the brushes, let them dry, and stood in the middle of the room. The studio was quiet. The paper on the table held a bird, a window, and a sky. All three of them were alive in a way I had not noticed before.

I looked around the room. There were more colors waiting. There were more brushes to try. There were more places to paint. I took a brush and dipped it into the jar. I began again.

At first, I feel the familiar rush of waking, of trying to be the person I want to be. But after the shower, the morning feels clearer. I have a routine I can follow without constantly wondering what to do. I can start slowly, then make a choice, and then make another.

I sit at the table and review the list of things I need to do. I do not need to finish them all at once. I need to get through them, however. The first task is to make a cup of tea. I choose a mug, fill it with water, and let the kettle work. I watch the water change color as it heats, and I notice the steam drifting into the air.

Next, I wash my hands and brush my teeth. I do not rush through the motions. I take the time to notice how my hands feel, how my breath feels, how the morning light enters the room.

Then I make breakfast. I cook the eggs and toast the bread, then eat slowly. I notice the flavors, the texture of the crust, the way the sunlight warms my hands. I do not eat in a hurry. I eat with the intention of nourishing my body and beginning the day properly.

After breakfast, I go for a short walk. I choose the path that leads toward the old oak. I notice the way the leaves change color, the way the branches spread across the path, and the way the light shifts as I move through the trees.

I compare the two paths. They are not exactly alike. One leads toward a quieter side of the house, while the other passes through a little garden and reaches the bench. I choose the bench path because it feels more purposeful. I want to arrive at the bench with something to show.

I sketch the old oak as I walk past it, capturing its rough bark, the curve of its branches, and the way the sunlight catches its leaves. I sketch the bench beneath the tree, noting its worn wood and the space around it. Then I sketch the mural, the figures, the colors, and the way it has changed over the years.

I sit on the bench and look at the mural. I notice the details I have missed, the parts of the scene I want to show more clearly. I sketch those as well.

Finally, I clean up. I put the dishes away, wipe down the table, and wash the brush. I make sure the path is clear and the garden is tidy.

As the day begins, I feel less overwhelmed. The routine is not a list of perfect tasks. It is a way of showing up. It is about making the small, deliberate choices of the morning, and then seeing what they create.

At the end of the morning, I sit on the bench again. The old oak is still there, and the mural is still there. The path has changed, and I have arrived somewhere I did not expect to be. I look at the sketchbook, then at the people around me. I am not beginning to look like the person I was before. I am beginning to look like the person I can be.

The day is not finished. It is only begun.

I had been sketching the initial outline for nearly an hour, tracing the curves of the face and the gentle slope of the shoulder. The watercolor work was still in its early stages—the washes were loose, the paper held a faint gray-green mist.

“Hold the brush in the corner of the hand,” I had told myself. “Keep the wrist loose enough to follow the paper without stealing the lines.”

I dipped into the blue, then the rose. A small circle of color appeared beside the face, then another beside it. I hesitated. Was the blue too strong? I softened it with a touch of white. The composition settled slightly. One hand held the brush, the other rested on the table, ready to begin.

“Don’t rush,” I said to myself. “Let the paint choose where to go.”

By the time I finished, the watercolor was almost complete. I leaned back and looked at the finished sketch.

The composition felt balanced, yet still full of possibility. I had captured the quiet energy of the room, the softness of the light, and the careful attention I gave to every small detail. I woke at 6:00 AM and made the morning routine while the sun felt soft and ready for the day. I ate breakfast before 6:30, then carried my notebook outside to the garden.

I started the opening scene with a small, ordinary girl who lost her favorite toy. A red ball had gone missing, and every toy in the neighborhood looked like it had been taken. The girl didn’t panic. She looked around slowly. She asked the squirrel, “Did you find it?”

The squirrel hopped over. “Yes, Miss, I found it.”

Then he did something the story never said aloud.

He put the ball under the tree.

The girl watched it. She smiled. “Thank you, squirrel.”

I wrote that line because a child can imagine a squirrel helping when another child is lost. The ball became more than a lost toy—it became a promise.

I paused at the page. The opening should feel alive, not just like a list of events. I want the girl’s fear to turn into curiosity. I want the squirrel’s kindness to feel earned, not handed over.

The children need to feel something before they read on. They need to believe that something ordinary—something small—can change a big moment.

I’m done with the opening scene.

content:
I woke at six. The sun had just crested the hill, and I was already out the door. After a quick shower and a cup of tea, I ate breakfast with my favorite muffin. By seven, I had finished the morning routine and made my way to my desk.

I was thinking about the opening scene for *The Little Star in the Well*. I imagined a small girl standing at the edge of the well, looking down at a bright star. She should feel curious, not scared. The story is about how a little person can change a big problem, one small thing at a time.

I drafted the opening scene again. The first paragraph is about the girl noticing the star. I changed the original opening because she should not already know the stars are special. That would make her seem like she already understands everything. Instead, I begin with something simple: she sees the star shining through the dark well.

For the dialogue, I used the girl’s voice.

“Are the stars above the well?” she asked.

The old well answered with a quiet sound, like the wind passing between the stones.

“Do the stars want to be seen?” the girl asked again.

The well did not answer in words. It answered with the light.

I wanted the child reader to hear the well speaking. So I made the dialogue sound gentle, with a pause at the end of each question. I also gave the stars a voice, but made their language softer than the girl’s.

I wrote:

“The stars want to be seen, little one,” the well said. “But their light is not ready to shine.”

“I know,” the girl replied. “But I have a wish.”

She held out a small hand.

“I wish the moon would come down here,” she said.

The well looked at the moon.

“Then come down and bring it down,” the well said.

The moon came down.

That’s the opening scene I wanted to show. A small girl who asks, a well that listens, and a moon that gives. I want the reader to feel that wonder without making it feel like magic belongs only to grown-ups.

I’ll revise the next paragraph and check the dialogue tags. They should feel natural for a child’s reader and easy to hear. I’ll also keep the story’s rhythm simple and warm.

By nine, I finished the opening draft and saved it. I’ll carry over the study with Jennifer Moore later this afternoon, then turn the next paragraph into a short scene for the children’s book.

content:
**The Little Lantern at the Door**

The house was quiet on the morning when it should have been awake.

The curtains held their breath, the floorboards didn’t creak, and the old kitchen lamp blinked once in the corner as if holding its last breath.

Then—the key turned.

A light appeared in the doorway.

Not from the window. Not from the street. It came from beneath the rug, where a tiny lantern had been hiding.

Inside, a small owl with two yellow eyes sat perched on the handle.

Its feathers were still fluffy, and its tail twitched once.

“Good morning,” the owl said. “Are you… ready to see the world?”

The door swung open.

A girl stepped through. She wore a coat of gray wool and carried a lantern that looked like it belonged to someone else.

“I’m ready,” she said. “But only when I’ve made sure the door is warm.”

The owl blinked. “Then you have a long walk ahead of you, little girl.”

The girl smiled. “I’m not afraid of the dark.”

She stepped inside.

The room was empty.

Except for the lantern.

And something else.

A small creature with a lantern of its own.

It was small enough to fit between two fingers. Its eyes were bright blue, and it was making a soft humming sound.

The owl hopped down.

“I don’t know where you came from,” the girl said. “But I can’t let you disappear now.”

“I’m not afraid of anything,” the owl replied. “Not unless you make me.”

The girl nodded.

She picked up the lantern.

“Come along,” she said.

The owl took a little step.

Then another.

And when they reached the door, the world was still waiting.

But the light was still there.

And something small was watching them.

content:
Good morning, everyone. I hope you’ve had a restful Wednesday. I’m still finishing the opening scene for *The Little Bear and the Midnight Moon*, and I want to make sure it feels warm, clear, and inviting.

I’ve been asking myself whether the opening should simply introduce the bear, or whether it should already show what the bear is feeling and what the story is about. I think the best approach is to begin with a quiet moment that makes the young reader want to keep turning the page. Let’s start with the bear waking up after a long winter sleep.

*The bear stirred. The moon was silver over the lake. Soft shadows moved across the mossy ground. He opened his eyes and found a small patch of sunlight on his paw.*

The bear looked down at his paw. It was warm. A little bird had returned to his nest.

*The tiny bird landed on the bear’s nose.*

“Good morning, little friend!” the bird chirped. “Did you sleep well?”

“I did,” the bear said. “I dreamed of the moon.”

The bird smiled. “Then you’ll dream again tonight.”

Before the bird could say anything else, the wind blew softly. The moon grew brighter, and a tiny shadow of a deer appeared in the tall grass.

*The deer did not move. He simply watched the bear.*

The bear’s eyes widened. “You’re awake,” he said.

“I am,” the deer replied. “I have been watching you since the beginning.”

The bear blinked. “I… did I dream about you?”

“I have been waiting for you to speak,” the deer said gently. “And now, little friend, you have.”

The bear closed his eyes. “I was afraid I was too old to make friends,” he whispered.

“You were not afraid,” the deer said. “You were afraid. That is how all children begin. And that is how all stories begin.”

The deer disappeared. The bird flew away. The bear stood alone in the quiet dawn.

For the first time, he smiled.

The opening scene should not explain everything. It should show the bear’s feelings, set the scene, and offer a small question to help the young reader begin wondering what is coming next. If the opening is this clear and warm, the rest of the book will have a gentle anchor.

I’ll revise the scene again this afternoon, and then I’ll carry over the study with Jennifer Moore later. I’m not tired, but I do need a little time to settle my notes. Please have a good rest today.

# Chapter 1: Matter and Chemical Change

## Key Concepts to Remember

1. **Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.** Atoms, molecules, and ions are the fundamental building blocks of matter.
2. **Chemical change** occurs when substances are rearranged into new substances with different properties. Common examples include burning, rusting, digestion, and photosynthesis.
3. **Physical change** alters the form or appearance of matter without changing its chemical identity. Examples include melting, freezing, evaporation, and dissolving.
4. **States of matter** include solid, liquid, gas, and plasma. Matter can change between these states.
5. **Conservation of mass**: In a closed system, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.
6. **Molecules and atoms**: Atoms combine to form molecules, which are held together by chemical bonds. Breaking or rearranging these bonds can create new substances.
7. **Chemical reactions involve breaking and forming bonds**: Energy is often released, absorbed, or neither depending on the reaction.
8. **Classification of reactions**:
   - **Synthesis**: Two or more substances combine to form a new substance.
   - **Decomposition**: A single substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances.
   - **Single replacement**: An element replaces another in a compound.
   - **Double replacement**: Ions exchange partners between two compounds.
   - **Combustion**: A substance reacts with oxygen, usually releasing energy.
   - **Acid–base**: Acids and bases react to form water and a salt.
9. **Solutions**: A solute dissolves in a solvent to form a homogeneous mixture. Solids, liquids, and gases can all be dissolved.
10. **Colligative properties**: The properties of a solution depend on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity. Examples include vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, and osmotic pressure.
11. **Equilibrium**: A reaction may proceed in both forward and reverse directions. The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
12. **Rate of reaction**: The speed at which reactants turn into products. It can be affected by temperature, surface area, concentration, catalysts, and collisions between particles.
13. **Catalysts**: Substances that speed up a reaction without being consumed or permanently changed. They lower the activation energy required for the reaction.

The room filled with the scent of wet paper, coffee, and something sharper—oak and rain. The instructor, Ms. Reyes, didn’t speak until we were settled, and then she began with a small exercise: write five sentences about the moment you’ve been waiting for most recently. We sat in quiet succession, each of us choosing a door—door number five, for one of us. The room held its breath.

Opening workshop overview: the session was not designed to be a performance, and yet it felt like one. Ms. Reyes reminded us that poetry is not about making the speaker speak more loudly, but about listening carefully to what is already being said. The opening poem was read aloud, then the class asked us to translate the same image into a different language, a different time, and without the original’s emotional shorthand.

The instructor introduced the session with a question that stayed with us: what do we carry inside us that we cannot speak? She showed how poetry can be a form of grief, a moment of recognition, or simply a way to name the things we have been holding together. By the end of the introduction, I felt less curious about how to “make” a poem and more curious about how to make a space where an image might finally speak.

I wrote down three things I found useful:

- The poem can begin without an answer.

- Revision does not make the poem stronger; it makes it honest.

I also wanted to begin with a draft poem about the moment I first realized that I was waiting for something I could not name. I had not been patient with myself. I had been impatient with the room, impatient with the question, and impatient with the possibility that another voice might arrive.

I finished the first draft in the corner of my mind, then returned it to the white page.

---

**The Door Number Five**

The classroom had a number on the door.

I had seen it written in pencil before, in the margins of a sentence I had never finished, in the corner of a photo taped to the wall. I had thought the number was a label, a small sign: *this is where you begin.* But now I understood that every number has a weight. Each one carries a story, and every story ends with silence.

I stood in front of the door and looked at my reflection in the glass. I was not the person who had been waiting. That person was not here. The person who was here was not the same person who had been waiting. I was the person who had been waiting long enough to begin to notice that the waiting was not the waiting itself.

The instructor had asked us to write five sentences about the moment we’ve been waiting for most recently. That was what I had written first.

I had written:

I had waited for the answer I had been given.

I had waited for the answer that could not be found.

I had waited for the question that had never been asked.

I had waited for the possibility that I might be wrong.

And then I had waited for the door to open.

It did.

The room held its breath.

I had not been waiting for anyone. I had been waiting for the thing inside me that had been waiting for something else.

---

Ms. Reyes began with a short poem about a woman who kept a map in her pocket. She said the map was not a place you could follow, but a place you were already inside.

She then paused and asked us to read the opening line aloud.

“*The moment you’ve been waiting for most recently,*” she said.

I read it. It sounded like a question. I read it again. It sounded like a secret.

The instructor did not explain what poetry was. She did not say what it could accomplish or how it might change us. She simply said:

> “Poetry is not a gift. It is a possibility.”

She showed us a photograph of a room filled with books, coffee cups, and something that looked like a door.

> “Every poet, I believe, carries a door in their body.”

She paused.

> “When you stand before a door, you are not looking for it. You are looking for yourself.”

I looked at the map in my pocket and saw it again.

We moved from the room back to the white page.

Ms. Reyes wrote:

> “A poem is a moment in time, held together by a single image.”

She did not explain the image. She simply asked us to choose one.

I chose the number five.

I wrote it down.

Then I wrote:

> Five is not a number. It is a threshold.

I wrote it again.

> It is where the first person begins.

I wrote it again.

> It is where the second person begins.

And it was not a poem I could read aloud.

I began to write.

The room did not stop listening.

The first line was not there.

The second line was not there.

The third line was not there.

The fourth line was not there.

The fifth line was there.

It was the most important one.

---

**Revision Notes**

I began the poem with the number.

The number gave the room a shape.

But the poem began with silence.

I wrote:

> The classroom had a number on the door.

Then I removed the last sentence.

Then I added:

> I had thought the number was a label.

Then I added:

> Each one carries a story.

Then I added:

> Every story ends with silence.

The poem was still unfinished.

But I had learned something:

A poem is not built by filling the page.

It is built by letting the page fill you.

The next draft will not be complete.

It will not be perfect.

It will not be ready.

It will be true.

I had never been more patient with myself.

I had never been more ready to begin.

I had never been more afraid of the possibility that the poem would not make sense.

And yet, I had found it.

I had found the moment.

I had found the door.

I had found the fifth line.

And I had begun again.

content:
The workshop instructor started with a poem about a house that finally fell down. The walls didn’t crumble; they gave up. I stared at the page. “That’s poetic,” the instructor said, tapping the pen against his knee. “You’re too polite to admit that.”

I said, “I’m not polite. I’m tired.”

The room went quiet.

I sat there for three minutes before I said it again. My throat felt like it was swallowing a stone. The instructor raised an eyebrow.

“Then why write about falling?” he asked.

I didn’t answer. I kept reading.

The first stanza was beautiful. The second was honest. But the third made me want to throw the notebook. I had been trying to make poetry sound interesting, and instead I had made it sound like I was apologizing for everything.

I left the room.

The instructor followed.

“Carlos,” he said, “you’re loud enough to be heard.”

I nodded.

He pointed to the page I was reading. “You’re not trying to be interesting. You’re trying to be real.”

I looked at him. Really looked at him. He was thirty-two. He had a poet’s eyes, but they were tired. The workshop was supposed to be about creativity. It was about becoming someone you weren’t.

I turned the page.

“Do you believe in poetry?” he asked.

“I believe in the work,” I said.

“Then why do you think anyone listens?”

I didn’t know if I was being rude or being honest. I was both.

“Because it’s hard,” I said.

He smiled. A real smile.

“Then you should write more.”

I nodded.

“Write more.”

I did not understand the instruction.

The Workshop Exercise

The workshop asked us to write a short poem from the inside of a habit.

I began with the one that begins everywhere: the one I learned at three years old, when I sat on a wooden chair and watched the floor grow dark beneath my feet.

This was not a poem about the floor, not really. It was a poem about the way my body had learned to make room for the dark.

I was still a child. I was still small. I was still believing that if I sat quietly long enough, the dark would shrink.

But the dark had not shrunk. It had taken me.

It had taken the way the floor felt beneath my feet.

It had taken the small, careful movements of the hands that held me when I was still too small to understand the world.

And it had taken the first time I had ever wanted to leave.

To leave was to become something else.

To leave was to become something that could no longer be named.

To leave was to become the dark.

The dark had not taken me.

The dark had been me.

It had been the chair.

It had been the floor.

It had been the way the sun came down through the window.

It had been the silence between the leaves.

content:
I woke up at 7, took the shower, and ate breakfast before heading out. I didn’t expect anyone to notice me, but today was different. I’m standing here in the workshop room reviewing the feedback I got from a few of my peers. Most of it is either polite or completely useless. I’m tired of being told what I should feel or how to write it.

One person said I should make my work more personal. Another complained that I sound too abstract. Neither of those comments made sense to me. I’m not trying to impress anyone. I’m trying to say what I’m feeling. Sometimes I want to scream into the room, but I know that’s not what I’m supposed to do. I’ve been told to be polite, and I’ve been told to be nice. But being nice doesn’t mean I can’t be loud, or mean I have to soften every voice.

I should probably stop listening to people who think they know my poetry. I do know my poetry. I wrote it when I was mad, afraid, lonely, or just bored. That’s the thing I’ve always liked about writing: it’s a private conversation with my inner self. I’m not here to perform. I’m here to hear myself.

One comment from the group dinner speaker was helpful. He said I should slow down and listen more carefully to the people around me. That made me pause. I was so frustrated, I didn’t notice the fact that I’d missed several of the poems in the collection. I should write again, not just defend myself.

I’m still not sure what I want to say next. I don’t want to be praised. I don’t want to be ignored. I just want to finish what I started.

The room was filled with the sound of pens tapping against notebooks, the low hum of a projector, and the distant click of a chair being pulled. I sat beside Elena, notebook open between us.

“You said the second exercise should be about something small,” she said. “Not the whole poem.”

and the quiet promise
that the water would
remember the order
of things before the kettle.

like a question

The first map had ink like wet slate.  
It showed the river, the valley,  
the house with three windows  
and one door that kept closing.

I followed it once.
